## 1. Core thesis

The temporary band makes **shared authorship possible without first making its members equally skilled, equally willing in every respect or permanently confident**. Airi's desire for something she can proudly name as a skill helps initiate the project, while a prize changes the peers' willingness and an adult assigns roles through a casual procedure that meets objections. The members then make actual practical contributions: clothing judgment, vocal labor, scheduling, physical endurance, theory study, turn-sharing, food and corrections. They want a joint event and one another's presence, yet what each person wants from the event differs. The ensemble's achievement therefore cannot be adequately described either as a professional product or as friendship which makes the work irrelevant. [A:L158–180,L194–210; P:L449–455,L498–504]

Technical difference becomes especially consequential when Airi treats difficulty as a threat to her place. Textbook delay, finger errors and inability to finish a full run are her stated obstacles, while the belief that friends will abandon her is her own interpretation of their offer to cover her. The peers reject a technically better replacement because the festival without Airi would not be enjoyable. They want this participant before they have solved the skill problem. Her resulting local self-liking does not cancel the work or future insecurity; it changes what failure can mean when wanted presence is distinguished from earned technical indispensability. [A:L168–180,L251]

The private endings keep this achievement temporary and plural. Airi mourns a practice place's rental ending while affirming love for familiar Sweets Club life; Natsu considers photographs but says documentation should not replace living the moment; Kazusa wants an imperfect first complete ensemble recording as a tangible memory; Yoshimi's successful private performance still leads to exhaustion when encores continue. Different completions preserve different goods. A record, shared food, a corrected musical turn and a local confidence can matter without establishing a lasting institution, perfect performance, permanent psychological cure or entitlement to every future audience. [P:L394,L439,L455; A:L197,L231]

Ordinary making is thus both an end and a source of claims on others. A particular song, outfit, texture, remembered crack in a voice or quiet performance audience need no public crisis to justify attention. Equally, practice fatigue, refused visits, privacy conditions and an unwanted reputational label are not negligible because the product is playful. The stronger thesis treats the members' wants as directed: a skill or joke offered by one person may be valued, questioned or refused by another, and real collaboration requires keeping those responses visible. [P:L428–455,L495–506; A:L166,L196–201,L216–231]
## 2. Longitudinal arc

The secure local sequence starts with an ordinary festival proposal and Airi's feeling that it may not be enough. Classmates explicitly deny rejecting her cafe idea and promise reciprocal visits; they provide no concrete replacement. She hears the question about an additional feature as a question about herself, and a station-square guitar helps trigger her own band idea. The adult's first participation is a failure of receiving: sweets are eaten before it is explained that the students wanted assessment, and both an apology and acknowledgment of incomplete explanation follow. These beginnings locate a desired difference inside an existing ordinary life, rather than prove that either the cafe or Airi has objectively failed. [A:L156–158]

Role allocation precedes full common understanding of motive. Yoshimi's views on visual presentation, Kazusa's voice and Natsu's remarks about rock become assignments in inward-tagged teacher lines. Yoshimi objects to the casual procedure while claiming ownership over clothing choices; Kazusa is reluctant to sing publicly, even as Airi sincerely wants to hear her. Natsu adapts to management, schedule and cleaning duties. The two-week deadline and semla prize help mobilize the project, but Airi privately seeks an answer that guarantees selection. This is not a jointly articulated mission whose participants all know the same reasons. [A:L158–162]

The studio and practice reveal the difference between participation and confidence. Sensei arranges a place, yet visits after Yoshimi explicitly says her refusal is not an invitation to do the opposite, and returns secretly after expulsion. Peer labor also has pressure: Natsu cannot maintain a demanded tempo, Airi tries to intercede and Kazusa maintains its necessity. Alone, Airi cannot yet say she enjoys playing; semla was an added justification for wanting a skill and becoming someone different. Her confidentiality request, two days of missed contact and later stated mistakes complete the local deterioration without requiring a clinical diagnosis. [A:L166–174]

The peers' search contains both wrong explanation and genuine wanting. They have noticed unequal amounts of pressure, theorize that loss of the prize is the problem and reject a technically better replacement because that festival would not be enjoyable. Their wish to help proceeds into a prospective theft plan, later actual detention and retrospective combat accounts. The latter are not a new complete reenactment, and the possible sanctions spoken earlier are not the final disposition. In the recognition scene, the founder/equality revelation, collective affirmation, Kazusa's apology and Airi's local statement of self-liking make changed reception visible. The forced disclosure and unprinted legal aftermath remain adverse and unfinished. [A:L170–180,L188]

The event's end provides chosen continuity rather than a total transformed identity. Airi chooses the current plan when the opening question returns, peers support the choice and a week of hard practice is retrospectively stated. She still refuses presidency; the group defers contacting Tsumugi until after the other performer's preparation. EVENT836010 is only a written video marker, so the full live itself was not watched or heard. The normal ending prints selection and prospective prize collection; the hidden ending prints reported praise, unwanted interviews and an actual explanation which is understood. These are branch-local completions, not two stages of one career. [A:L184–205,L237]

Private continuations complicate any fixed growth ladder. Kazusa can value a first uninterrupted complete recording while retaining its skipped parts and cracked voice. Yoshimi can genuinely finish and be praised for a selected solo piece while becoming exhausted under extra requests. Natsu's exercise report, practice-room restoration and independent film choice show different kinds of ongoing work. Airi's rental-ending account explicitly accepts that the band must end for now and asks what next. The argument can follow these local tails without assigning every variant and branch a unique date or calling the end a failure because it is finite. [P:L394,L439,L455,L495–501; A:L237]
## 3. Public/private self

Airi's public proposal and private desired self are different pieces of authority. “Semla” is a real peer attraction and later prospective prize, not a meaningless decoy. But Airi explains to Sensei that she wanted an instrument or any skill she could proudly call hers, fears using friends and wants change. The readers hear this before the friends form their mistaken theory. That unequal distribution of knowledge permits a causal comparison: their action can be devoted while their diagnosis is false. It does not establish that Airi's imagined hostile words were actually spoken or that public optimism was calculated deceit. [A:L158,L168–174,L250]

Her late anxiety includes actual skill deficits as she describes them, but they do not exhaust the problem. The friends' offer to cover her is interpreted as a risk of abandonment; she also knows they do not actually mean it that way. A technical solution alone cannot settle the question of being wanted. The subsequent affirmation is more precise because peers reject a skilled substitute and want her presence. At the same time, new difficult music and a lyric task do not make the practical deficits disappear. Both meaningful recognition and unfinished capacity survive the ending. [A:L174–180]

Private self-disclosure has its own audience. Airi asks for confidentiality; later she does not initially want the confession told to friends, and helpful disclosure occurs against her plea. She receives a positive recognition scene, while the analysis retains the manner in which knowledge becomes available. Her rental-ending MomoTalk tail again asks privacy for an embarrassing conversation. Those conditions are neither proof she wants permanent secrecy from every peer nor obstacles whose removal is automatically justified by a good ending. [A:L168,L176–180; P:L394]

Kazusa's public role coexists with controlled private expression. She did not choose the vocalist role, yet refuses to abandon it and asks for a reliable rehearsal partner who will not tease her. The narrator judges her skilled; stage relaxation remains unfinished. She distinguishes this practice from wanted lively karaoke afterward. Elsewhere a genuine compliment makes the complimenter uncomfortable, a mask's motive remains unprinted and a rejected image should not be voiced. Public participation therefore expands repertoire without transferring ownership of her reputation to peers or teacher. [P:L428; A:L220–223]

Yoshimi insists on a distinction between an assignment and her own contribution. Clothing advice should support her selection, not replace it; anticipated autograph fame is conditional and its actual accidental use on a bill produces staff rebuke and embarrassment. Her private musical piece is chosen and prepared distinctly from the band's, with sitting used to avoid mistakes. Narrated success and gratitude do not erase objections to mockery, continued encores or later searches for the first song. A wanted cool public image, manual choices and a fatigued body belong to the same person without one explaining the others away. [P:L449–455]

Natsu's insight is sometimes generous, sometimes provisional and sometimes not what recipients assume. She says a plan is perfect but later admits nobody knows the real performance result; she wants another shared occasion while Yoshimi wants someone to stop her; at one point she simply asks lunch preferences and peers assume another odd plan. Private music and leisure likewise include denial of the stress explanation, fear of moving dust and a deliberate quiet cinema visit for new stimulation. Neither visionary fool nor infallible romantic organizer accounts for these different purposes. [A:L199–202,L229–230; P:L492–501]
## 4. School/club role

The band grows out of an informal club with no fixed leader or decision rule. Airi's founderhood is revealed later with her preference for equality, while the others propose leadership and she refuses. An adult's quick role assignments and the practical schedule do not create a fully voluntary or formally governed new organization. Informal role power remains real: it determines who must sing, choose clothes, maintain rhythm, study, clean, use the room and be available for practice. The institutional analysis must retain that power without inventing a charter or filling the refusal of presidency with an enacted appointment. [A:L158–160,L180,L186]

Equality is not sameness of skill or effort. Members need theoretical foundations, correction of posture, a chance to take a turn and ways to handle fatigue. Kazusa recognizes she has monopolized an opportunity and gives Airi space; Airi asks for feedback. Yoshimi's local family chant is laughed at and she gives way to the familiar version even though Airi validates regional difference. These acts show both actual making of parity and a pressure toward group norm. A claim of equal friendship cannot substitute for examining who gets time, who adjusts and whose taste or expression is treated as normal. [A:L195–199]

The setting also distributes resources and consequences. Sensei's studio arrangement is useful; Airi's later rental ending makes that place finite. Tea Party festival resources and JTF detention affect the peers' attempted help, while Ichika's hope of indulgence remains a forecast rather than a formal pardon. An institutional phone report is not an eyewitness account of all force. The band can be a real setting of growth, pleasure and access without proving that every resource use, breach or sanction was settled appropriately. [A:L166,L174–180,L188; P:L394]

Role interpretation remains contestable after practice begins. Natsu's rhythmic responsibility and daily endurance work do not rank instruments; Yoshimi wants skill as a distinction from ordinary school life; Kazusa worries about public nerves while liking present singing; Airi wishes to experiment without fearing failure with friends. The analysis can value each motive without declaring that ordinary personhood is inadequate or all participants desire professionalization. A performed role is a local practical responsibility, not a total identity or career appointment. [P:L501,L504; A:L216,L223–224]

The branch endings test how external attention can exceed the role the group wanted. Normal selection supports a plan to collect the prize, not completed collection or revenue. In the hidden ending, interview demands raise unwanted questions about name and agency; narration says explanation occurs and is understood. No signed representation, professional contract or universal publicity consent follows. Their ability to clarify the band is a real outcome precisely because public recognition is mixed happiness and burden, rather than an unquestioned reward. [A:L204–205]
## 5. Ordinary life

The new activity is wanted in ways that coexist with the old. Airi's taste and conversation are not deficiencies the band must replace: she explicitly loves the familiar club and does not want only band life. The disappearing practice place hurts because it held a different possibility, not because the old life is worthless. The future remains a question after the local acknowledgment that this project ends for now. This is an ordinary ending with real loss and anticipation, independent of winning a prize or acquiring office. [P:L394]

Yoshimi's clothes are made meaningful through actual judgment. She specifies pieces and coordination, knows why an all-peer shopping trip might in her view derail the plan and retains ownership while asking for sincere advice. Actual payment and packing are printed; a complete journey home is not. In the event the shirts are being worn, while Natsu's suggestion that a cat comparison caused Kazusa's wearing is denied by Kazusa. Neither a joke nor a friend's stylistic preference is an objective design law. The clothes materialize participation without eliminating disagreement about what participation should look like. [P:L449; A:L219]

Instrumental competence is also desired on its own terms. Yoshimi chooses and prepares a private piece, asks not to be mocked, adjusts by sitting and actually finishes music the narrator praises. The requested encores are eventually accepted but leave her exhausted; the complete tail thanks attentive listening while objecting to later pressure. Wanted recognition and bodily cost cannot be replaced by a simple before-and-after graph of confidence. Her own first-audience statement belongs to that local performance, not an independently verified career beginning. [P:L455]

Kazusa's rehearsal and leisure are explicitly distinguished. Reliable private practice is for an assigned role she decides not to abandon; lively karaoke afterward is a wanted different activity. She can value teacher's company while asking about its availability, and a later spoon-sharing misunderstanding causes embarrassment despite enjoyable cake and a whole-message taste confirmation. A good practice or shared sweet does not become a general touch, teasing or attendance license. The ordinary pleasure explains why she returns, while the limits explain what that return does not authorize. [P:L428–431]

Her LP is especially important because imperfection is part of the intended object. She denies having released an album and explains she commissioned tangible records from data. A worker supplies actual turntable assistance. They listen to the first uninterrupted complete ensemble run: early playing, skipped portions and a cracked voice belong in the wanted memory. She includes teacher's karaoke and her tambourine because the contribution belongs to the recollection. This is not a poor substitute for a professional recording; it is a differently valued object. Prior capture/distribution permission and acoustic properties remain unverified, while the local listening is represented. [P:L437–439]

Natsu's ordinary support of music crosses body, room and attention. She seeks a new stimulus when practice stalls and chooses a revival film at a quiet time, then becomes so absorbed that popcorn goes uneaten and is given to teacher. Another urgent practice-room message concerns a feared crawling thing which teacher finds to be moving dust; the search has dismantled drums, help with reconstruction is narrated to the end and cookies are shared. Daily running and a wish to anchor rhythm coexist with teacher's recurrent sleepiness despite coffee. Exercise, help, film and food are real ordinary labor and enjoyment; no resulting drum mastery or clinical fatigue cure is printed. [P:L495–501]

Food does not simply vanish when music begins. Practice displaces snacking, Airi proposes eating together and Kazusa brings sweets to exhausted peers. Semla call-and-response renews motivation according to participants, while Natsu's hypnosis analogy is not verified mind control. Airi hopes disappearing mint sweets mean converts but Yoshimi reports Airi ate them herself. Taste is a wanted shared invitation, not a fact that everybody already shares it. The band's making includes breaks and appetite without converting every sweet into a technical recovery mechanism. [A:L198,L213–214,L226]

The final ordinary good is inhabiting a finite time. Natsu recognizes the temporary project and weighs photographs, then chooses some documentation plus living the moment so the record does not consume everyday life. Actual photographs taken or permission granted are not supplied by this statement. Kazusa's LP later chooses a concrete memory with its own permission seam, and Airi's ending names a lost place. These are related answers to impermanence, not evidence one member has found a universal preservation method or that the band must continue forever to have mattered. [A:L231; P:L394,L439]
## 6. Crisis behavior

Technical difficulty is not merely a test to pass before the true plot begins. The demanded tempo, theoretical pain, finger errors and unequal endurance affect recipients during practice. Airi tries to intercede for Natsu, Kazusa emphasizes rhythm, members study foundations and coordinate turns; these are real contributions with differing reasons. A leaderless group's procedure can allocate burdens even without a formal command, so equality and affection do not make all demands effortless or all errors psychologically caused. [A:L166,L174,L195–199]

When Airi withdraws, the peers' response is active but epistemically incomplete. Kazusa and Natsu had noticed pressure without raising it; Yoshimi had not. The letter's promise of a better replacement is quoted to friends, and they delegate searching while constructing a semla theory. Readers already know why that theory is wrong. Their rejection of a substitute is strong contrary evidence to Airi's fear of technical expendability, while their proposed harmful means do not become permissible through devotion. The source's false explanation is part of the causal argument, not a flaw to silently correct. [A:L168–172,L250–251]

The outcome has several kinds of closure. Airi is found through a late-night encounter, the peers are in detention, an explanation and recognition occur, and more difficult music with wanted lyrics is offered. Kazusa apologizes for having assumed Airi was fine; the founder/equality statements contextualize the peers' desire to keep her. The local self-liking ending is achieved. A final pardon, restitution, every force consequence, permanent confidence and unrestricted disclosure consent are not. Those limits do not weaken the positive recognition; they specify its actual extent. [A:L174–180,L188]

Quieter practice crises and completions remain required. A finger cut and bandage shortage prompt rest alongside continuing competitive invitations; another breathless session stops for the day. Study is felt to help, followed by more work and a groaning afterstate which does not explicitly establish sleep or mastery. Group gymnastics yield a declared completed maneuver and celebration, yet Kazusa still asks why they are doing it. Completing a maneuver while losing its musical purpose is a serious contrary endpoint to the claim every group activity proves coordination. [A:L207–214]

Local image protection can impose a cost on another member. Airi's energetic embarrassment produces a sound; Kazusa blames Natsu incorrectly, and Airi's parenthetical apology does not publicly correct the attribution. Airi's earlier fear is not grounds to suppress this adverse local act. Similarly, technical joy in stick-spinning meets Kazusa's request not to do it publicly or with them, and a desire for future occasions meets Yoshimi's wish to stop Natsu. The band's positive making is more legible when these small recipient failures and refusals survive beside its larger reconciliation. [A:L225,L228–229]
## 7. Sensei relationship

Sensei supplies actual material and interpretive assistance: assessments after the initial eating mistake, help finding music, a studio, searching, listening and difficult conversations. The private scenes include practical clothing assistance, study, rehearsal, drum reconstruction and participation in remembered music. These contributions are substantial. They are not proof that the adult predicted the entire arc, composed every student choice or made peer initiative unnecessary. The event itself begins with incomplete explanation and apology, and Tsumugi retains independent artistic judgment and a question about reassurance. [A:L158–180; P:L428–455,L498]

The role-assignment episode requires exact limits. Teacher's inward-tagged wording transforms answers into roles; not every inward line can be assumed externally heard in the same manner. Yoshimi objects to casual assignment, Kazusa is reluctant and Airi sincerely wants her voice. Those student purposes exist independently of teacher's cleverness. Subsequent acceptance or practice cannot turn the original choice into a wholly self-chosen arrangement. Teacher support has to be evaluated against the kind of participation each student later claims and refuses. [A:L160,L241; P:L428,L442]

The practice intrusion is a direct adverse action. Yoshimi explicitly clarifies that “do not come” is not an invitation to reverse the words; teacher nevertheless comes, uses affection as teasing pressure, is expelled and later secretly returns. A useful room arrangement does not buy unrestricted access to unfinished work. The ordinary stakes—being heard before ready, control over presentation, embarrassment—are enough to make the refusal consequential. No expected comic personality provides contrary consent. [A:L166]

The confidentiality case is similarly mixed. Teacher offers not to force Airi back and receives her difficult motive; later useful disclosure occurs after she initially refuses telling friends and pleads against the explanation. The private rental-ending tail again makes confidentiality explicit. Her local relief and peers' recognition are real ends, but they cannot certify the manner of disclosure as freely requested. The argument separates help, knowledge and recipient control rather than making one benevolent narrative intention settle all three. [A:L168,L174–180; P:L394]

Private musical audiences also exert pressure. Yoshimi's selected piece actually finishes and narration praises it; encores extend effort into exhaustion. Kazusa's practice partner is wanted under a promise against teasing, while later karaoke is her different pleasure. Natsu's steady rhythm and caring wait do not prove antecedent permission for teacher's sleeping shoulder contact or complete comprehension of her account. These are meaningful relationships because companionship and contrary recipient boundaries both remain, rather than because every adult response is ideal. [P:L428,L455,L501]

The record includes teacher as a contributor without making that inclusion a permission receipt. Kazusa wants teacher's karaoke voice and her tambourine in the LP memory; represented surprise establishes no prior recording or distribution assent. A worker rather than Sensei supplies the turntable expertise. Shared authorship is therefore distributed across students, adult contribution, material helpers and a recipient who does not perfectly know how the object was made. The public product is not a signed professional agreement or complete technical authority of the teacher. [P:L437–439]
## 8. Major peer relationships

Airi's authorship is more than the proposal and less than command over everybody. She wants her friends present, founds the ordinary club with parity in mind, seeks a skill and asks for feedback. They affirm they stay because she is Airi, and she still declines presidency. A person can originate a wanted project and receive help without holding its participants as instruments of a private self-improvement program. Her fear of using them is her own assessment; the analysis checks their actual reasons and adjustments instead of confirming or simply dismissing that fear. [A:L168,L180,L194–197,L251]

Yoshimi contributes style, guitar labor, a distinct wish for skill and a right to have wants put into words. Her opinion about peers' clothing remains an opinion, while actual selection, payment, packing and worn shirts are practical outcomes. Teasing over a local family chant, research into teeth-guitar technique she explicitly does not want to perform, and the accidental bill autograph reveal limits between aspiration, manual action and how peers interpret an image. She is not merely a comic reward-seeker whose protests can be discarded after she joins. [P:L449–455,L473–475; A:L196,L216–219]

Kazusa contributes reliable singing, bass/vocal work and attention to a member losing practice time. She takes the assigned task seriously but still expects nerves, dislikes an imposed public title and asks that unwanted images not be expressed. Her record selects a flawed shared performance for memory, so the criterion of value is not only technical excellence. The same person can maintain rhythm as necessary and later value early mistakes. Those are different contexts of responsibility and recollection, not proof a contradiction must be eliminated. [P:L428,L439,L442; A:L166,L197,L220–223]

Natsu's management and drumming include routine cleaning, exercise, scheduling and needs for space. She denies ranking instruments and works on endurance, while her perfect-plan rhetoric is qualified by admitted uncertainty. Stick-spinning and group gymnastics can be joyful, but peers may not find them adequate musical work or welcome stick-spinning: Kazusa asks that it be done neither publicly nor with them. A simple request for lunch preferences can also be misread by a group accustomed to her odd ideas. This reciprocal shorthand is both useful familiarity and a source of error; it cannot become a reliable motive decoder. [P:L498–506; A:L211–214,L223,L228–231]

The members' tastes and bodies resist being standardized by collaboration. Theory is harder than playing for some; posture matters; fatigue differs; snacks can be displaced; a wanted chant or shirt prompts dispute. Airi validates Yoshimi's regional expression, while the group ultimately uses the familiar chant. Kazusa gives up a monopolized turn and proposes attention to posture. These practical acts achieve something without guaranteeing that every expression receives equal status. The ensemble can value their making while asking who continually adjusts to the norm. [A:L195–199]

Tsumugi is an independent artist and recipient, not a tool who certifies the club's worth. She declines to dictate somebody else's motive and warns against fearful music in her own voiced artistic terms; later she contributes more difficult music and wants the heroine to write lyrics. Her challenge to whether reassurance postpones insecurity is not canceled by her confidence in them. The club also respects her preparation by postponing contact until after the performance. Those two directions—help offered and limits respected—are more exact than a mentor's endorsement as proof of objective musical merit. [A:L162,L178,L186]

Outside helpers and audiences likewise have their own positions. A shop worker helps with the turntable; private music is heard and evaluated in narration; hidden-ending audiences are reported praising and demanding interviews, then the actual explanation is understood. Festival security and JTF have reported custody/action scopes, with no completed pardon from hopeful informal assistance. An unnamed retrospective accuser in012 is not joined to Reisa merely because named Reisa later visits in020. The ensemble needs these boundaries to avoid making every surrounding role an unqualified witness to the band's growth. [P:L437–439; A:L174–188,L201,L205,L239–241]
## 9. Language/voice

“Voice” here is written register and represented musical judgment, not personally heard performance. EVENT836010's video marker is fully received writing while its audio and motion are unreceived. Printed Tsumugi lyrics and crowd enthusiasm are textual descriptions, not reenacted violence. Private narrators' judgments of songs, Kazusa's appreciated record noise and named genres are part of the literary representation; they do not establish independent acoustic measurements or our evaluation of acting. [A:L184–186,L235; P:L428,L439,L455]

The rhetoric of competence and wanted identity is not a stable technical scale. Airi seeks something she can proudly name as a skill; Yoshimi wants a distinction from ordinary life; Natsu calls a plan perfect and then admits nobody knows; Kazusa can like her current singing while expecting nerves. Their actual words express local aims and competing standards. An analyst may compare those standards without elevating one participant's definition into a certified grading scheme for everybody. [A:L168,L202,L216,L223–224]

Purpose language can also conceal a mistaken collective explanation. Semla really motivates the peers, yet “Q.E.D.” does not make their theory of Airi's disappearance correct. Her prior private explanation and later recognition provide the contrary witness. The corpse and vomiting-blood rhetoric are not actual deaths or medical events; hypnosis is Natsu's analogy for a motivating call-and-response, not verified mental control. These distinctions protect both comic vitality and factual causality. [A:L168–184,L199,L214,L250]

Image and name language has particular recipients. Kazusa rejects Cath Palug and unwanted voiced images; Yoshimi's regional chant is laughed at but Airi affirms difference; an autograph is corrected from a band-logo misunderstanding. The band does not gain permission to define members through a nickname because they perform together. Conversely, a personally used local manager label is not a professional contract. Written warmth, gratitude or future invitation must remain separate from agreement to every reputational role. [A:L172,L196,L199,L220; P:L434,L449–452]

Source actor seams qualify exact speakers without destroying the recoverable collective argument. Consequential sites in assignments, practice, recognition, regional chant, written labels and retrospective reports remain identified in the current checkpoint. Secure founderhood, Airi's final voiced line and broader interaction are used beside qualified collective speech, rather than repairs which assign every rebuke or affirmation to a named member. UIEvent progress/shop/mission modes, repeated special passages and blank profiles do not create additional enacted performances or a costume-growth chronology. [A:L239–241; P:L409,L442–444,L473–475,L504–506]
## 10. Competing readings

**“The prize was the real motive, so musical desire is only decoration.”** Semla actually changes peer response and remains a wanted prospective reward. Airi explicitly says it was an added justification; Yoshimi wants a skill, Kazusa wants a record and Natsu values the finite common goal. The stronger account keeps food and music as different goods distributed across people, rather than making the false semla diagnosis true or erasing the peers' appetite after exposing it. [A:L158,L168–180,L202–204,L216,L231; P:L439]
